title: ‘I’m not a cyclist, I’m a human being’: Trevor Ward column
content:
Cyclist
‘I’m not a cyclist, I’m a human being’: Trevor Ward column

Apparently the residents in the cyclo-tourism heartland of Calpe in Spain are getting fed up with us. The local council is investigating whether the economic benefits of professional and amateur riders visiting for winter training camps outweigh the inconvenience caused by riders ‘flouting traffic regulations’ and ‘blocking roads’.

Meanwhile a study from Denmark, perennially hailed as a global model for urban and utilitarian cycling, found that everyday riding had declined during the past five years. Which is a bit like hearing sales of Irn Bru are plummeting in Scotland or Spaniards are going to bed earlier.

My cycling DNA has elements of Danish commuter mixed with bits of cyclo-tourist. Like the Danes, I often use my bike for doing errands or attending appointments, and although I’ve never worn a suit and tie on my bike, I regularly dress in ‘civilian’ clothes, particularly if I don’t want to cause a scene attending Arbroath FC games.

I’d fit into the Copenhagen cycling template quite easily. Cycling is (or was?) such an accepted, everyday routine there that individuals riding bikes are defined by much more than their choice of transport. ‘Student’, ‘parent’, ‘plumber’ and ‘prime minister’ are just some examples. But I also regularly travel abroad to ride my bike on scenic roads with guaranteed sunshine. And I hope the locals can see beyond my Lycra and oversized sunglasses and recognise an incorrigible romantic fleeing an interminable Scottish winter who misses his cat. 

I don’t want them to dismiss me as ‘a cyclist’. Such a sweeping term doesn’t do justice to my particular relationship with my bike and my reasons for riding it. To paraphrase John Merrick in the film The Elephant Man: ‘I’m not a cyclist, I’m a human being!’

An old pal recently messaged me on Facebook to ask if he could introduce me to one of his friends because ‘he’s also a cyclist’, as if we belong to some obscure religious cult and therefore share the same beliefs and lifestyles. I didn’t respond. I would never want to know someone purely because they were a cyclist. If they were also a fellow journalist, fan of ’90s shoegaze or agreed that Chinatown was the greatest movie of all time, fair enough. But just because they ride a bike?

What if they ride it really fast and just want to talk about their FTP or VO2 max? I’ve got more in common with a cabbage.

If you should introduce yourself to me as ‘a cyclist’, please don’t expect a knowing nod, a masonic handshake and an unqualified sense of fraternity. Chances are I’ll find your views on the Middle East much more revealing – and interesting – than your finishing time at the Etape Loch Ness. And I’ll feel much more empathy with you if you suffered cold and rain on your morning commute to work rather than severe cramp on your club’s annual hill climb.

An elderly neighbour who knows I’m a cyclist recently showed me a tatty, worn piece of paper from his teenage years as an apprentice painter. I feared it would be his winner’s certificate from some long-defunct race but it turned out to be a court summons for cycling home from work without lights on a January evening in 1967. He was fined £2 for being a repeat offender.

I’m no lawbreaker, but that’s the kind of cyclist I can bond with – and I’ve arranged to go for a ride with Bruce if he can borrow his daughter’s e-bike.

American writer William Saroyan often rode his bike. He was also a Pulitzer Prize and Oscar-winning novelist and screenwriter who said, ‘I was not yet 16 when I understood a great deal from having ridden bicycles for so long, about style, speed, grace, purpose, value, form, integrity, health, humour, music, breathing and, finally and perhaps best of all, the relationship between the beginning and the end.’

That’s the kind of rider I want to be – not a cyclist at all.
